promptText: According to the chapter, what does Big O notation actually describe about an algorithm?
options: The worst-case upper bound on how running time or memory grows as input size increases, ignoring constants and lower-order terms
The exact number of milliseconds an algorithm takes on a given machine
The average-case running time only, never the worst case
The best-case running time an algorithm can achieve
explanation: Big O is hardware-independent and describes the shape of growth (a worst-case bound), which is why an O(n) algorithm beats O(n^2) for large n regardless of machine speed; Theta is the tight bound and Omega the lower bound, but Big O dominates interviews.

promptText: A candidate writes two separate (non-nested) O(n) loops over the same array, one after the other. What is the overall time complexity, and why?
options: O(n), because sequential loops add rather than multiply
O(n^2), because any two loops touching the same array multiply
O(log n), because the second loop can skip elements already seen
O(n^2), because two loops always mean nested iteration
explanation: The chapter explicitly warns that loops multiply only when nested; separate sequential loops just add (O(n)+O(n)=O(n)) — a common mistake is assuming any two loops over n automatically means quadratic.

promptText: The chapter states O(n log n) is the best achievable complexity for general comparison-based sorting. Under what condition can you legitimately claim a faster sort?
options: When the input has known range constraints allowing a non-comparison sort like counting or radix sort
When using recursion instead of iteration
When the array is already partially sorted, since Big O ignores best-case scenarios
It's never possible; O(n log n) is a hard limit for every sorting algorithm
explanation: Comparison-based sorts can't beat O(n log n), but counting/radix sort avoid comparisons entirely by exploiting a bounded or known value range, achieving O(n) under those constraints.

promptText: Why is ArrayList.add() described as 'amortized O(1)' rather than simply 'O(1)'?
options: Most calls are O(1), but occasionally the backing array is full and must be copied to a larger array (O(n)); because resizing is rare and doubles capacity, that cost averages out over many adds
Because add() always takes O(n) time but interviewers round it down to O(1) for simplicity
Because ArrayList uses a hash table internally which occasionally rehashes
Because the JVM's garbage collector pauses execution during every add() call
explanation: The chapter stresses that 'amortized O(1)' is not the same as 'always O(1)' — a single add can spike to O(n) during a resize, but spreading that rare cost across all adds gives amortized O(1); HashMap rehashing is the analogous spike there.

promptText: Per the chapter's guidance on choosing between a HashMap and a HashSet, which fits a problem asking 'how many times does each element appear'?
options: HashMap, using each distinct element as a key mapped to its running count
HashSet, since sets are optimized for counting duplicates automatically
HashMap, but only because HashSet cannot store duplicate values internally
Either works identically since both give O(1) average lookup
explanation: The chapter distinguishes HashSet for O(1) membership/dedup ('have I seen this?') from HashMap for O(1) lookup of an associated value such as a count, via map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) — counting needs a value attached to the key, which only a map provides.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend java.util.ArrayDeque over java.util.Stack for implementing a stack in interview code?
options: Stack extends the legacy synchronized Vector class, making it slower, while ArrayDeque is the modern, unsynchronized stack/queue implementation
Stack does not support a pop() method, only remove()
ArrayDeque is the only Java class that supports LIFO ordering
Stack cannot be used to solve the valid-parentheses problem
explanation: The chapter explicitly notes Stack extends Vector and is synchronised/slower, calling ArrayDeque 'the modern stack and queue in Java' for both push/pop and offer/poll operations.

promptText: The chapter notes that inserting already-sorted data into a plain BST degrades it toward a linked list with O(n) operations. How do Java's TreeMap and TreeSet avoid this exact failure mode?
options: They are implemented as self-balancing Red-Black trees that rebalance on insert/delete, guaranteeing O(log n) regardless of insertion order
They store elements in a hidden HashMap internally and only sort them when iterated
They reject sorted input and throw an exception, forcing the caller to shuffle it first
They fall back to binary search on a resized array whenever the tree becomes unbalanced
explanation: The chapter ties BST degeneration directly to why self-balancing trees exist: Red-Black trees maintain balance invariants through rotations on every insert/delete, so O(log n) holds even for already-sorted input, unlike a naive BST.

promptText: A problem asks for a pair of numbers summing to a target using the two-pointer technique (indices moving from both ends). What precondition does this technique require to run correctly in O(n)?
options: The array must already be sorted, so moving lo up or hi down predictably increases or decreases the sum
The array must contain only positive integers
The array must have an even number of elements
The target value must be zero
explanation: Two-pointer relies on monotonic behavior: in a sorted array, incrementing lo can only increase the sum and decrementing hi can only decrease it, letting each pointer move safely without missing the answer — on unsorted input this guarantee fails, which is exactly why the unsorted Two Sum problem instead uses a HashMap.

promptText: In the sliding-window solution for 'longest substring without repeating characters,' why does the technique achieve O(n) instead of the O(n^2) of checking every substring directly?
options: The left and right pointers each only move forward, so every character enters and leaves the window at most once across the whole scan, instead of every substring being recomputed from scratch
It uses a HashMap instead of a HashSet, which is inherently faster for character storage
It sorts the string first, allowing binary search for repeated characters
It only checks substrings of even length, halving the total work
explanation: The window expands (right++) and shrinks (left++) but neither pointer ever moves backward, bounding total pointer movement by 2n — this avoids the repeated recomputation from scratch that makes the brute-force substring check O(n^2).

promptText: After Floyd's fast/slow pointers meet inside a linked-list cycle, how does the chapter say you locate the exact node where the cycle begins?
options: Reset one pointer to the head, then advance both pointers one step at a time — they meet again exactly at the cycle's start
The meeting point itself is always the cycle's start
Restart slow at the head and fast at the meeting point, then move only fast until it returns to the head
Count the total steps taken so far and divide by two to get the start index
explanation: This is Floyd's second phase: resetting one pointer to head and advancing both one step at a time makes them converge precisely at the cycle entry point, a distinct fact from merely detecting that a cycle exists.

promptText: The chapter calls out a common bug when validating a binary search tree. What is that bug, and how is it fixed?
options: Only comparing a node against its immediate children instead of checking it against a valid (min, max) range inherited from all its ancestors
Using recursion instead of an iterative stack-based approach
Forgetting to check whether the tree is empty before starting
Comparing node values with == instead of a range check, which only matters for Integer objects outside the -128..127 cache range
explanation: A node can be valid relative to its immediate parent yet still violate the BST property relative to a grandparent further up; the fix threads shrinking (min, max) bounds down the recursion, or equivalently checks that an in-order traversal is strictly increasing.

promptText: To find the kth largest element in an array, the chapter recommends maintaining a min-heap of size k rather than a max-heap of the whole array. Why does a min-heap work here?
options: Keeping only the k largest values seen so far in a min-heap means the smallest of those k sits on top, ready to be evicted when a larger value arrives — leaving exactly the kth largest on top once all elements are processed
Java's PriorityQueue can only be configured as a min-heap, so there is no other option
A max-heap would give the wrong answer because it cannot hold more than one element at a time
Min-heaps sort their contents in O(1) time while max-heaps require O(n log n)
explanation: This is the chapter's 'counter-intuitive but key' point: a size-k min-heap discards its smallest element whenever size exceeds k, so after processing all elements the root is the kth largest; a max-heap of the full array would instead need extra work to dig down to the kth element.

promptText: The chapter warns that Dijkstra's algorithm fails on graphs with negative edge weights. What exactly causes this failure, and what should be used instead?
options: Dijkstra permanently finalizes a node's shortest distance the moment it's popped from the priority queue, but a later negative-weight edge could still produce a shorter path to it — Bellman-Ford should be used instead
Negative weights cause Java's PriorityQueue to throw a runtime exception, so BFS should be used instead
Dijkstra's distance array cannot represent negative numbers, so Kruskal's algorithm should be used instead
Negative weights automatically make the graph cyclic, so topological sort should be used instead
explanation: Dijkstra's greedy assumption is that once a node is popped with the current minimum distance, no shorter path can appear later; negative edges break that assumption, whereas Bellman-Ford re-relaxes edges repeatedly and correctly handles negative weights (short of negative cycles).

promptText: The greedy rule for interval scheduling ('always pick the interval that ends earliest') provably gives the optimal answer, but the chapter warns that greedily picking the largest coin first fails for coin change with arbitrary denominations. What distinguishes these two cases?
options: Interval scheduling has the greedy-choice property, justifiable by an exchange argument, while arbitrary coin denominations lack it — a locally optimal coin choice can block a globally optimal combination, which is exactly why coin change is instead solved with DP (dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a-coin])
Greedy always works for counting problems but never for optimization problems
Coin change is NP-hard, so no algorithm, greedy or otherwise, can solve it optimally
Interval scheduling only works on small inputs, whereas coin change scales to arbitrarily large ones
explanation: The chapter's senior-level distinction is that greedy is only correct when the greedy-choice property can be proven (e.g. via an exchange argument showing the greedy pick is never worse); with denominations like {1,3,4} for amount 6, always taking the largest coin first can strand the search in a suboptimal total, which is precisely why coin change needs the DP recurrence instead.

promptText: In the space-optimized 0/1 knapsack solution, the weight loop iterates from cap down to wt[i] (descending). What would change if that inner loop instead iterated ascending from wt[i] up to cap, and why?
options: It would silently turn the solution into the unbounded knapsack / coin-change variant, allowing each item to be reused multiple times, because dp[w - wt[i]] could already reflect the current item having been counted earlier in the same pass
Nothing would change; the loop direction is purely a stylistic preference with identical results
It would throw an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException because w - wt[i] could go negative
It would force the algorithm to compute the full 2D dp[i][w] table instead of the 1D dp[w] array
explanation: Descending iteration guarantees dp[w - wt[i]] still reflects values from before item i was considered, enforcing 'use each item once'; ascending iteration lets an already-updated dp[w - wt[i]] (which may already include item i) feed forward into dp[w], effectively permitting unlimited reuse — the exact mechanism separating 0/1 knapsack from the unbounded variant used in coin change.
